title: Lighter Than Cotton Candy: Meet the Fluffiest Planets Ever Found!
summary: Hold a piece of cotton candy in your hand — it's mostly air, right? Now imagine a planet that's even lighter than that fluff! Astronomers just found two such worlds, and they're blowing scientists' minds. These planets, named TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, are about the size of Jupiter, our solar system's biggest planet. But here's the crazy part: Jupiter is like a heavy rock compared to them. Jupiter's density is 1.33 grams per cubic centimeter. TOI-791 b is only 0.038 grams per cubic centimeter — that's 35 times lighter! Cotton candy is about 0.05 grams per cubic centimeter, so these planets are literally fluffier than the treat at a fair. They orbit a star 1,110 light-years away, which means the light we see from them started traveling when knights were still around on Earth. The two planets are locked in a special dance: for every five orbits of the inner one, the outer one goes around three times. Their gravity tugs on each other, which helped scientists figure out their masses. The discovery started with volunteers — regular people like you! — who spotted dips in starlight while looking at data from NASA's TESS satellite. Then professional astronomers used telescopes, including one in Antarctica, to watch the planets' long transits (each over 11 hours!). Antarctica's dark winter nights let them observe without the sun interrupting. Scientists think these "super-puff" planets have huge, puffy atmospheres of hydrogen and helium, like balloons. They probably formed far from their star where it was cold enough for gas to pile up. There are only four other systems with multiple super-puffs known, so this is a super rare find. What's next? More telescopes will study these weird worlds to figure out how they got so fluffy!
why_it_matters: Understanding strange planets like these helps us learn more about our own solar system and could even give clues about how Earth formed.

background_read: Astronomers search for new planets by looking at stars and waiting for the light to dim when a planet passes in front. NASA's TESS satellite (a space telescope launched in 2018) does this from space, but volunteers on Earth also help by checking the data.
Sometimes scientists use telescopes in extreme places like Antarctica, where long winter nights let them watch stars for many hours without the sun rising.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers and volunteer citizen scientists.
WHAT: The discovery of two super-puff planets, TOI-791 b and c, that are fluffier than cotton candy.
WHERE: Orbiting a star 1,110 light-years away; observed by telescopes including one in Antarctica.
WHY: To understand how such light planets form and why they are so rare.

perspectives.description: These discoveries show that even regular people can help find new planets, making science open to everyone.
Super-puff planets are so far away that we can't visit them, so studying them only gives us pictures and data, not hands-on exploration.
Scientists are excited but also puzzled because there are only a few known systems with multiple super-puff planets, so each one is a rare puzzle.
